title: OAuth2 and JWT
description: Learn OAuth2 and JWT for authentication and authorization in microservices.

data.text: OAuth2 and JWT are the de facto standards for authentication and authorization in microservices. Google, GitHub, and Stripe all use OAuth2 for delegated authorization and JWT for stateless token-based authentication.

OAuth2 is an authorization framework that allows third-party applications to obtain limited access to user accounts. It defines four grant types: authorization code (most secure), client credentials (machine-to-machine), implicit (legacy, avoid), and password (avoid if possible).

JWT (JSON Web Token) is a compact, URL-safe token format used to represent claims between parties. JWTs are self-contained: they carry all the information needed to authenticate a user, eliminating the need for database lookups.

data.title: JWT Structure
items: Header: Algorithm and token type (HS256, RS256)

data.title: JWT Security
data.text: Never store sensitive data in JWT payloads. JWTs are base64-encoded, not encrypted. Use RS256 (asymmetric) for public key verification. Always validate signatures and expiration.

data.title: Example: JWT Token Structure
data.content: A JWT token with header, payload, and signature.
data.code:
# JWT Token (base64url encoded parts)

# Header
{
  "alg": "RS256",
  "typ": "JWT",
  "kid": "key-123"
}

# Payload (claims)
{
  "sub": "user-123",
  "email": "alice@example.com",
  "roles": ["user", "admin"],
  "iat": 1705278000,
  "exp": 1705281600,
  "iss": "https://auth.example.com"
}

# Signature
# HMAC-SHA256(base64url(header) + '.' + base64url(payload), secret)

data.caption: OAuth2 authorization code flow
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant A as Auth Server
    participant R as Resource Server
    C->>A: Authorization Request
    A->>C: Authorization Code
    C->>A: Exchange Code for Token
    A->>C: Access Token + Refresh Token
    C->>R: Request with Access Token
    R->>C: Protected Resource

items.question: Should I use OAuth2 or OpenID Connect?
items.answer: OAuth2 is for authorization. OpenID Connect (OIDC) is built on OAuth2 and adds identity. Use OIDC when you need authentication.

items.question: Where should I validate JWTs?
items.answer: At the API Gateway is best. It offloads auth logic from internal services. Pass the user identity in headers to backend services.

items.question: What about token revocation?
items.answer: JWTs cannot be revoked once issued (they are stateless). Use short expiration times and refresh tokens. For immediate revocation, maintain a blocklist or use opaque tokens.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: OAuth2 is the standard for delegated authorization
Validate JWTs at the API Gateway
Use RS256 for better security than HS256
data.takeaway: OAuth2 and JWT are the foundation of microservices authentication; implement them correctly.
